title: The Autonomic Nervous System
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers how the autonomic nervous system reaches smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands: where sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons sit, which transmitter and receptor act at each synapse, and how the receptor's G protein decides the response. It then applies that wiring to three high-yield problems: the oculosympathetic pathway and Horner syndrome, the parasympathetic ganglia of the head, and autonomic dysreflexia after high spinal cord injury. Board questions usually give a set of signs and ask you to locate the lesion, or give a receptor and ask you to predict the effect. Both tasks depend on tracing the two-neuron chain correctly.
prerequisites: Spinal cord cross-sectional anatomy, including the lateral horn and ventral roots (NE-3)
Cranial nerve nuclei and the course of CN III, VII, IX, and X
G protein-coupled receptor signaling: Gs, Gi, Gq, cAMP, IP3, and DAG
Smooth muscle excitation-contraction coupling through calcium-calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase

connections.to: Cardiovascular physiology (CV units on pacemaker activity and blood pressure control)
connections.how: Beta1 and M2 receptors set heart rate and contractility, and sympathetic tone to the splanchnic bed sets much of total peripheral resistance.
Chromaffin cells are modified sympathetic postganglionic neurons whose epinephrine output depends on cortisol-induced PNMT.
Cranial parasympathetic fibers travel on branches of the trigeminal nerve, so gland function helps localize lesions of CN VII and IX.
A superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor at the lung apex produces Horner syndrome by compressing the sympathetic chain.
Bladder filling and emptying depend on beta3 and alpha1 sympathetic and M3 parasympathetic receptors, and bladder distension is the most common trigger of autonomic dysreflexia.

terms.def: An autonomic neuron with its cell body in the brainstem or spinal cord whose thinly myelinated axon ends in an autonomic ganglion.
An autonomic neuron with its cell body in a ganglion whose unmyelinated axon ends on the target tissue.
The lateral horn of spinal gray matter from T1 to L2 that contains sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies.
The connection, present only from T1 to L2, that carries myelinated preganglionic fibers from a spinal nerve into the sympathetic chain.
The connection, present at every spinal level, that returns unmyelinated postganglionic fibers from the chain to a spinal nerve.
A visceral nerve; thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves carry sympathetic fibers, while pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) carry parasympathetic fibers.
A sympathetic ganglion on the front of the abdominal aorta (celiac, aorticorenal, superior and inferior mesenteric) where splanchnic preganglionic fibers synapse.
An adrenal medullary cell, derived from neural crest, that acts as a postganglionic neuron and secretes mainly epinephrine into the blood.
The group of sympathetic preganglionic neurons at about C8 to T2 whose axons ascend to the superior cervical ganglion to supply the eye.
Ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and, depending on the lesion level, facial anhidrosis caused by interruption of the oculosympathetic pathway.
Episodic severe hypertension in spinal cord injury at or above T6, caused by an uncontrolled spinal sympathetic reflex to a stimulus below the lesion.
Increased responsiveness of a target to its transmitter after loss of innervation, partly from receptor upregulation.

blocks.text: Autonomic output to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands uses a two-neuron chain. A preganglionic neuron in the brainstem or spinal cord sends a thinly myelinated B fiber to a ganglion outside the central nervous system, where it synapses on a postganglionic neuron whose unmyelinated C fiber reaches the target.
Sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow

Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies form the intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) of segments T1 to L2. Their axons leave in the ventral root and pass through a white ramus communicans into the paravertebral chain. White rami exist only at T1 to L2, because only those segments hold preganglionic cells. In the chain a fiber may synapse at its own level, travel up or down the chain to synapse at another level, or pass straight through as a splanchnic nerve.

Fibers that synapse in the chain return postganglionic axons through gray rami communicantes to all 31 pairs of spinal nerves, reaching sweat glands, arrector pili, and vessels of the body wall and limbs. Fibers for the head ascend to the superior cervical ganglion, and postganglionic cardiopulmonary nerves from the cervical and upper thoracic ganglia supply the heart and lungs. Abdominopelvic splanchnic nerves (greater, lesser, least, and lumbar) carry preganglionic fibers to the prevertebral ganglia on the aorta. The adrenal medulla is the exception to the two-neuron rule: preganglionic fibers end directly on chromaffin cells, which release hormone into the blood.
Parasympathetic (craniosacral) outflow

Parasympathetic preganglionic cells lie in brainstem nuclei of CN III (Edinger-Westphal nucleus), CN VII (superior salivatory nucleus), CN IX (inferior salivatory nucleus), and CN X (dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, plus cardiac neurons near the nucleus ambiguus), and in the lateral gray matter of S2 to S4. The vagus supplies the thoracic viscera and the gut as far as about the distal third of the transverse colon, the end of the midgut. Pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2 to S4 supply the descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, bladder, and erectile tissue. The ganglia sit beside or within the target, so preganglionic fibers are long and postganglionic fibers short.

Ganglion position sets the reach of each division. One sympathetic preganglionic fiber diverges onto many postganglionic neurons at several chain levels, and the adrenal medulla adds circulating epinephrine, so sympathetic activation is widespread. Parasympathetic divergence is small, so a pupil can constrict without any change in gut motility. Most viscera receive both divisions, but most blood vessels, sweat glands, arrector pili, and the adrenal medulla receive sympathetic fibers only, so their activity is graded by raising or lowering sympathetic discharge.

blocks.caption: Pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic; every other splanchnic nerve is sympathetic.

blocks.predict: A surgeon cuts one sympathetic chain between the stellate and T2 ganglia. Does hand sweating change, and is the eye affected?
blocks.explain: Hand sweating is largely lost. Upper limb preganglionic fibers leave at about T2 to T6 and must ascend the chain to the stellate and cervical ganglia, whose gray rami join the brachial plexus; the cut blocks that ascent. The eye is usually spared because most oculosympathetic fibers leave at T1, above the cut.
blocks.check: White rami only at T1 to L2; fibers ascend the chain to other levels.

sections.title: Transmitters, receptors, and G proteins at autonomic synapses

blocks.text: Every autonomic ganglion uses the same synapse: preganglionic neurons of both divisions release acetylcholine (ACh) onto neuronal nicotinic receptors (NN), ligand-gated channels permeable to Na+ and K+ whose opening produces a fast excitatory postsynaptic potential. Adrenal chromaffin cells carry the same receptor, which is why they behave like postganglionic neurons. NN receptors differ in subunits from the muscle-type NM receptors, so a ganglionic blocker silences both divisions without paralyzing skeletal muscle.

At the target, parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release ACh onto muscarinic receptors, and most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine (NE) onto adrenergic receptors. Eccrine sweat glands used for heat loss are the main exception: their sympathetic postganglionic fibers release ACh onto M3 receptors, so muscarinic blockade produces hot, dry, flushed skin. The adrenal medulla secretes about 80% epinephrine because its phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which methylates NE, is induced by cortisol reaching it through intra-adrenal portal vessels.

blocks.title: Transmitter and receptor at each synapse
rows: NE on alpha or beta receptors
None: preganglionic fiber ends on chromaffin cell (ACh on NN)
Epinephrine (about 80%) and NE released into blood
ACh on M2 (heart) or M3 (smooth muscle, glands)
blocks.caption: Every ganglion is cholinergic and nicotinic.

blocks.text: Adrenergic and muscarinic receptors are G protein-coupled. Gq activates phospholipase C, which cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol (DAG); IP3 releases Ca2+ from the endoplasmic or sarcoplasmic reticulum and DAG activates protein kinase C. Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and activating protein kinase A (PKA). Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, and its beta-gamma subunits open K+ channels and inhibit Ca2+ channels.

blocks.title: Autonomic receptors and their G proteins
rows: Vasoconstriction, pupil dilation (dilator pupillae), internal urethral sphincter contraction
Less NE release from terminals, less insulin release
Increased heart rate, contractility, and AV conduction; renin release
Bronchodilation, skeletal muscle arteriolar dilation, uterine relaxation, glycogenolysis
Central nervous system and enteric neurons, gastric secretion
Slower SA node firing and AV conduction
Gland secretion, gut motility, bronchoconstriction, detrusor contraction, miosis, accommodation
blocks.caption: Alpha1 and M3 share Gq; alpha2 and M2 share Gi; beta receptors use Gs.

blocks.title: How alpha1 stimulation contracts vascular smooth muscle
steps: NE binds alpha1 receptor
Gq activates phospholipase C
IP3 releases Ca2+ from sarcoplasmic reticulum
Ca2+-calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase
Phosphorylated myosin forms cross-bridges
Arteriole narrows; resistance rises
blocks.caption: M3 contraction of bronchial, gut, and detrusor muscle uses the same pathway.

blocks.text: The same messenger can act in opposite directions. In cardiac muscle, PKA phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels and phospholamban, so beta1 stimulation strengthens contraction; in smooth muscle, PKA phosphorylates and inhibits myosin light chain kinase, so beta2 stimulation relaxes it. In the SA node, M2 beta-gamma subunits open acetylcholine-activated K+ channels and lower cAMP, which flattens phase 4 and slows the heart. Most vessels lack parasympathetic supply, yet ACh dilates them through endothelial M3 receptors that release nitric oxide. Presynaptic alpha2 receptors provide negative feedback on NE release. Acetylcholinesterase ends ACh action; NE is removed mainly by reuptake through the NE transporter and degraded by monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase.

blocks.predict: Predict heart rate, pupil size, and skin temperature after a large dose of atropine, a muscarinic antagonist.
blocks.explain: Heart rate rises because M2 blockade removes vagal tone. The pupil dilates and accommodation fails because sphincter and ciliary muscle M3 receptors are blocked. Skin becomes hot and dry because sympathetic cholinergic sweat fibers act through M3, so sweating stops.
blocks.check: The synapse table and the sweat gland exception.

sections.title: The oculosympathetic pathway and Horner syndrome

blocks.text: Sympathetic fibers to the eye and face supply the dilator pupillae (alpha1), the superior tarsal muscle (smooth muscle attached to the levator palpebrae superioris), and facial sweat glands and arterioles. They travel in a three-neuron chain, and a break at any link removes sympathetic tone on the same side.

blocks.title: The three-neuron oculosympathetic pathway
steps: First order: posterolateral hypothalamus
Descends uncrossed through lateral brainstem and cervical cord
Synapses in ciliospinal center, C8 to T2
Second order: exits mainly at T1, white ramus
Ascends chain over lung apex, through stellate ganglion
Synapses in superior cervical ganglion near carotid bifurcation
Third order: plexus on internal carotid artery
Through cavernous sinus, with V1, to dilator and tarsal muscle
blocks.caption: Facial sweat fibers follow the external carotid artery instead.

blocks.text: Each sign follows from a lost target. Losing the superior tarsal muscle drops the upper lid only 1 to 2 mm, because the levator, supplied by CN III, still works. Loss of the inferior tarsal muscle lets the lower lid rise slightly, narrowing the fissure so the eye looks sunken (apparent enophthalmos). Miosis results from the parasympathetic sphincter acting unopposed; anisocoria is greatest in dim light, when the normal pupil dilates and the affected one lags, yet the affected pupil still constricts briskly to light. In congenital Horner syndrome the affected iris is often lighter, because iris pigmentation needs sympathetic input during development.

Whether the face sweats depends on the lesion level, which makes anhidrosis a localizing sign. First- and second-order lesions interrupt sudomotor fibers before they branch off at the carotid bifurcation, so the face is dry. Third-order lesions on the internal carotid spare the external carotid fibers, so facial sweating is spared except perhaps over the medial forehead.

blocks.caption: Facial sweating separates postganglionic lesions from the others.

blocks.text: A Pancoast tumor is a carcinoma in the superior pulmonary sulcus at the lung apex. Growing upward, it compresses the stellate ganglion and second-order fibers over the pleural dome and invades the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8, T1), causing medial arm pain and wasting of intrinsic hand muscles. In internal carotid dissection, blood enters the arterial wall through an intimal tear, and the expanding hematoma stretches the carotid plexus, giving an acute painful Horner syndrome without facial anhidrosis; narrowing or thrombus can cause stroke.

blocks.title: Horner syndrome compared with oculomotor (CN III) palsy
blocks.caption: In Horner syndrome the smaller pupil is abnormal; in CN III palsy the larger one is.

blocks.title: Locating a Horner lesion from the history
blocks.text: A 52-year-old smoker has 2 mm right ptosis, a right pupil 2 mm smaller than the left in dim light, a dry right face, and inner right arm pain with weak finger abduction. Step 1: mild ptosis with a small reactive pupil means Horner syndrome. Step 2: the dry face places the lesion before the carotid bifurcation (first or second order). Step 3: no brainstem signs, but medial arm pain and weak interossei implicate the lower trunk (C8, T1), which lies beside second-order fibers at the lung apex. Conclusion: a second-order lesion, likely a Pancoast tumor.

Cranial parasympathetic preganglionic fibers leave the brainstem in CN III, VII, and IX and synapse in four ganglia. The postganglionic fibers then ride on branches of the trigeminal nerve to reach their targets. Sympathetic and sensory fibers also pass through these ganglia, but only the parasympathetic fibers synapse there. Learning each route as nucleus, nerve, ganglion, carrier branch, and target makes lesion questions predictable.

rows: Inferior division of CN III (branch to inferior oblique)
Greater petrosal nerve, then nerve of the pterygoid canal
Branches of V2; zygomatic branch to the lacrimal nerve
Lacrimal gland (tears); nasal, palatine, and pharyngeal glands
Chorda tympani, joining the lingual nerve (V3)
Directly to the submandibular gland; via the lingual nerve to the sublingual gland
Otic (below foramen ovale, medial to V3)
Tympanic nerve, tympanic plexus, lesser petrosal nerve
blocks.caption: CN VII serves two ganglia (tears and two salivary glands); CN IX serves only the parotid.

blocks.text: At the ciliary ganglion the targets act through M3 receptors. Contraction of the circular sphincter pupillae constricts the pupil. Contraction of the ciliary muscle moves the ciliary body inward, which slackens the zonular fibers and lets the elastic lens round up for near vision. In the pupillary light reflex, optic nerve fibers project to both pretectal nuclei, and each pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so light in one eye constricts both pupils (direct and consensual responses).

Gland function localizes facial nerve lesions along the canal. The greater petrosal nerve leaves at the geniculate ganglion, the chorda tympani leaves lower in the facial canal, and only motor fibers remain beyond the stylomastoid foramen. The parotid is never affected by a facial nerve lesion, even though the nerve runs through the gland, because its secretomotor supply comes from CN IX.

blocks.title: Localizing a facial nerve lesion by tears, saliva, and taste
blocks.text: Three patients have complete right facial weakness. Patient A also has a dry right eye, loss of taste on the anterior two thirds of the right tongue, and reduced submandibular flow: the lesion is at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion, before the greater petrosal nerve leaves, as with a tumor in the internal acoustic meatus. Patient B tears normally but has lost taste and submandibular flow: the lesion lies in the facial canal after the greater petrosal nerve leaves but before the chorda tympani leaves. Patient C has weakness alone: the lesion is at or beyond the stylomastoid foramen, as with a parotid tumor. Parotid flow is normal in all three.

Misdirected regrowth of cholinergic fibers explains three classic syndromes. In Frey syndrome, after parotid surgery, cut postganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve regrow into the sympathetic cholinergic sweat glands of the overlying skin; both systems use ACh on muscarinic receptors, so eating causes sweating and flushing over the cheek. In crocodile tears, after a proximal facial nerve injury, salivary fibers regrow along the greater petrosal pathway, so eating causes tearing. In Adie tonic pupil, damage to the ciliary ganglion, often after a viral illness, leaves a dilated pupil with a poor light response; regenerating fibers meant for the ciliary muscle reach the sphincter, so the pupil constricts slowly during sustained near focus (light-near dissociation), and the denervated sphincter becomes supersensitive to a dilute cholinergic agonist.

sections.title: Autonomic dysreflexia after spinal cord injury

blocks.text: Autonomic dysreflexia is a sudden, potentially dangerous rise in blood pressure in a person with spinal cord injury at or above T6, triggered by a stimulus below the lesion. It usually appears after spinal shock resolves and segmental reflexes return, weeks to months after injury. Resting systolic pressure in these patients is often low, about 90 to 110 mmHg, because tonic sympathetic drive from the brainstem is lost, so a rise of 20 mmHg or more above baseline is significant, and pressures above 200 mmHg can occur. Bladder distension is the most common trigger; bowel impaction, pressure injuries, ingrown toenails, and labor are others.

The T6 level matters because of the splanchnic circulation. The greater splanchnic nerve (about T5 to T9) and the lesser and least splanchnic nerves control the splanchnic vascular bed, the largest pool of resistance and capacitance vessels in the body. With a lesion at or above T6, most of that outflow lies below the injury and is cut off from brainstem control. With a lower lesion, the brainstem still governs splanchnic outflow and can dilate that bed to offset vasoconstriction in the legs.

blocks.title: From a full bladder to a hypertensive crisis
steps: Bladder distends below the lesion
Visceral afferents enter cord below the injury
Segmental sympathetic preganglionic neurons fire massively
Splanchnic and lower-body vessels constrict
Blood pressure rises sharply
Baroreceptors signal the nucleus tractus solitarius
Vagal outflow slows the heart
Descending inhibition blocked at the lesion; pressure stays high
blocks.caption: The reflex continues until the stimulus is removed, because the brainstem can act only above the lesion.

blocks.text: Below the lesion, isolated cord segments still respond to segmental afferent input. Without descending inhibition the reflex is exaggerated, and changes after injury add to it: sprouting of primary afferent terminals in the cord, and increased sensitivity of denervated vessels to alpha1 stimulation. The carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) baroreceptors detect the rise. The brainstem responds in the two ways still open to it: vagal slowing of the heart, which works because the vagus leaves the brainstem and never passes through the injured cord, and withdrawal of sympathetic tone above the lesion. Neither can reach the constricted vessels below, so the pressure stays high.

The signs divide at the lesion. Above it, vasodilation produces flushing, nasal congestion, and sweating, and the pressure surge with cerebral vasodilation produces a pounding headache and sometimes blurred vision. Below it, sympathetic discharge produces pale, cool skin and piloerection. Bradycardia is typical but not universal. Uncontrolled episodes can cause intracerebral hemorrhage, seizures, myocardial ischemia, and pulmonary edema.

blocks.title: Autonomic dysreflexia compared with neurogenic shock
rows: After spinal shock resolves (weeks to months)
Hours to days after acute injury above about T6
Uncontrolled spinal sympathetic reflex below the lesion
Loss of sympathetic tone with intact vagal tone
blocks.caption: Both need a high lesion and both may show bradycardia, but the blood pressure moves in opposite directions.

blocks.predict: Two patients with complete injuries, one at C6 and one at T10, each develop a distended bladder. Which one becomes severely hypertensive, and why?
blocks.explain: The C6 patient. Below C6 the whole splanchnic outflow is cut off from the brainstem, so the reflex vasoconstriction is unopposed. At T10, splanchnic outflow from about T5 to T9 remains under brainstem control, so baroreflex withdrawal of sympathetic tone dilates the splanchnic bed and limits the rise.
blocks.check: The paragraph on why the T6 level matters.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology set the wiring. Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are confined to T1 to L2, so any target outside those levels, including the eye, depends on fibers that travel through the chain, which is why a lung apex tumor or a neck injury can disturb the pupil. Neural crest gives rise to the chain ganglia, the parasympathetic ganglia, and the adrenal chromaffin cells, so a chromaffin cell behaves like a postganglionic neuron. Cranial parasympathetic fibers borrow trigeminal branches, which turns gland function into a map for localizing lesions of CN VII and IX.

Physiology and pathology follow the receptors. One transmitter can contract or relax a tissue depending on whether Gq, Gs, or Gi carries the signal, and the same receptor logic predicts the effects of toxins and drugs used to probe the system. Horner syndrome and autonomic dysreflexia are both disorders of interrupted descending sympathetic control, with opposite results: loss of tone at a single target in one, and an unrestrained segmental reflex in the other. The limits are that localization by signs is probabilistic, not every patient shows every sign, and reference values such as the dysreflexia threshold vary between sources.

summary: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons lie in the T1 to L2 lateral horn and synapse in chain or prevertebral ganglia; parasympathetic preganglionic neurons lie in CN III, VII, IX, X nuclei and S2 to S4 and synapse near the target.
White rami (T1 to L2) carry preganglionic fibers into the chain; gray rami return postganglionic fibers to every spinal nerve.
All autonomic ganglia use ACh on NN receptors; sympathetic targets use NE except sweat glands (ACh on M3), and the adrenal medulla secretes mostly epinephrine.
Alpha1 and M3 use Gq to raise Ca2+; beta receptors use Gs to raise cAMP; alpha2 and M2 use Gi to lower cAMP, and M2 also opens K+ channels in the SA node.
Horner syndrome is ipsilateral mild ptosis and miosis greatest in dim light, from a break in the three-neuron hypothalamus to C8 to T2 to superior cervical ganglion to carotid plexus pathway.
Facial anhidrosis marks a first- or second-order lesion; a third-order lesion such as carotid dissection spares facial sweating and is painful.
A Pancoast tumor causes a second-order Horner syndrome with lower brachial plexus pain and hand weakness.
Ciliary (III) controls pupil and lens, pterygopalatine (VII) tears, submandibular (VII) submandibular and sublingual saliva, and otic (IX) parotid saliva.

Autonomic dysreflexia needs a lesion at or above T6, so the splanchnic bed escapes brainstem control; a stimulus below the lesion causes severe hypertension with baroreflex bradycardia and flushing above the lesion.

verify: Sympathetic outflow is given as T1 to L2; some texts extend it to C8 or L3. Confirm the levels NABNE expects.
The ciliospinal center is given as C8 to T2 with most fibers leaving at T1; some sources say T1 to T2 or T1 to T3.
The vagal territory is given as ending at about the distal third of the transverse colon; sources also say the splenic flexure.
The adrenal medullary output of about 80% epinephrine follows Guyton and Hall; other texts give 80% to 85%.

The autonomic dysreflexia threshold (a systolic rise of 20 mmHg or more above baseline) follows current consensus definitions and may differ in older texts; the T6 cutoff is also sometimes stated as above T6.
Upper limb sympathetic preganglionic levels (about T2 to T6) vary among anatomy texts (T2 to T8 also appears).
Some eccrine sweat glands (palms, soles) and apocrine glands also respond to adrenergic stimulation; this chapter teaches the thermoregulatory cholinergic rule.
Confirm whether NABNE expects eponyms such as ciliospinal center of Budge, Muller muscle, Jacobson nerve, Frey syndrome, and Adie pupil, or only the descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: autonomic-outflow (spinal cord with white and gray rami, chain, prevertebral ganglia, and craniosacral outflow) and oculosympathetic-pathway (three-neuron chain from hypothalamus to eye).
